newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Philippines starts over.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Philippines starts over.

text.p: The central bank of the Philippines has decided to take bids all over again for its planned Yankee bond issue, Asian debt traders learned on Friday.
The issue, which was expected to carry tranches of 30- and 100-year maturities, was scuppered in April.
At that time, the central bank said the issue was postponed because of poor market conditions.
But the issue was controversial even before the last-minute decision to postpone it, with bankers complaining about the bidding process and subsequent moves on allocations and fees.
The Philippines central bank has denied that the Yankee bond had problems with infighting among arrangers.
"It is an opportune time for BSP (central bank) to re-launch the bond," the bank said.

The six investment banks that had been chosen to lead the first deal -- Salomon Brothers, JP Morgan Securities, Citicorp, Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley and ING Barings -- have been invited to bid on the second.
Salomon was lead manager and bookrunner for the first deal.

The first bidding process was a beauty pageant, in which the contestants were sized up based on a variety of factors, including the pricing they could offer and their distribution capabilities. The bonds were to be sold on a best-effort basis.

Sources said the new mandate will be awarded based on price only. Furthermore, the issue now will be a "bought deal," meaning that the underwriters will have to absorb any of the paper they can't sell.
"With the chance of getting stuck with 100-year paper, you can bet the pricing will be fairly competitive," said one syndicate manager.
Bids reportedly are due on June 16.
Bankers said the six investment banks are probably still keen on getting the mandate because Philippine credits continue to sell well, despite tight pricing.
With the exception of Salomon, none of the leads were available for comment. Salomon Brothers said it still intended to participate in the bidding process.
In other news, Greater Beijing 1st Expressways priced its 144a debt issue overnight on Thursday, increasing it to US$288 million from US$275 million.
The seven-year tranche carried a 9.25 percent coupon and was issued at 99.796 to yield 287.5 basis points over Treasuries.
The 10-year tranche, which was increased by US$13 million to US$188 million, carried a 9.5 percent coupon and was issued at 99.365 to yield 312.5 basis points over the benchmark.
Chinese issuers are in favour with lenders.

Bank of China is expected to launch a US$200 million floating-rate note (FRN), Agricultural Bank of China a US$120 million floating-rate certificate of deposit (FRCD) and Guangdong Development Bank is tippped to tap the market again having just completed a US$50 million FRCD.
PT Enseval is in the market with a US$100 million revolving credit four-year facility.
Looking ahead, Kookmin Bank plans a US$100 million FRN, with a three-year maturity and puts and calls at the end of year one. Shinhan Bank is planning a US$150 million five-year 144a bond.
In Hong Kong, the market was relatively quiet, despite nervousness that the handover will effectively close the market down because of the public holidays to mark the event.
"It's black Friday," said one bank treasurer.
The handover meant Asian borrowers had to wrap up deals in the next two weeks, or wait until mid to late July, he said.
Banks expect a flurry of activity ahead of the handover.
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty on July 1 after more than 150 years of British rule, and the occasion will be marked by public holidays on June 30 and July 1 and 2.
